messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 18
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Tax Consultant
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is an 18-year-old African American man who started his first year working as a junior tax consultant while trying to present himself as composed and capable. The assault happened several months earlier, when an older man he knew through a casual social connection forced sex on him in an unfamiliar apartment after a night when voices had already been raised. What has stayed with Kwame is not a smooth story but a series of sharp fragments: the sound of shouting in another room, the abrupt noise of a door opening and then slamming shut, the sense of being trapped alone with another man who was physically closer and stronger than he was. When he talks about it, he does not give a long narrative. He returns instead to flashes of the doorway, the man’s body blocking his exit, and the sick, vivid taste in his mouth that seems to come back exactly as it was then.

In the weeks afterward, Kwame found that ordinary situations began to feel charged with danger. If a stranger moved toward him on the street or in the lobby outside his office, he felt his body brace before he had time to think. Being touched unexpectedly, even lightly on the shoulder by a coworker trying to get his attention, made him jolt hard and turn with alarm. He had also begun avoiding unfamiliar places because he felt he could not judge who might be there or whether he could get out quickly. What frightened him most was being alone with men. He had come to believe that once he was in that position, things could change in an instant and he would again be overpowered before anyone noticed.

Those beliefs were constantly sharpened by the things that set him off. At work, if a conference-room door opened suddenly behind him or someone let a heavy door slam down the hall, his chest tightened and he scanned for who was near him. If he heard men arguing loudly in the office or outside on the street, he became immediately alert to exits, distance, and whether he was trapped. The trigger did not stay just a sound for long. A slammed door could pull up a bright image of that apartment entrance; shouting could bring back the whole emotional force of the assault before he could place why he was suddenly panicking. Sometimes he would also get the taste from that night in his mouth so distinctly that he had to swallow repeatedly to convince himself he was in the present.

The memories themselves made the world feel even narrower. Because they came mostly as pictures rather than as a story he could hold at a distance, a glimpse of a closing office door or the sight of two men standing too close in a hallway seemed to carry the event inside it. There were moments when no image appeared at all and yet the fear hit him with full intensity, as if his body had recognized danger before his mind had. After episodes like that, he became even more watchful around doors, male coworkers, and strangers, noticing every change in volume or movement around him. He started arranging his workday around what felt safer: avoiding unfamiliar client sites, lingering near open areas rather than small offices, and finding reasons not to be in a room alone with male colleagues.

That watchfulness had begun to feed back into the memories. Once Kwame was already tense and scanning for danger, even minor things seemed to gather force. A stranger stepping toward him to ask a routine question could make him feel under threat, and in that heightened state the assault returned in fragments—first the visual flash of the doorway, then the taste, or sometimes just a wave of dread with no picture at all. He noticed too that when he was most keyed up, he became more sensitive to the exact things that reminded him of what happened: the pitch of male voices, the sound of a door moving, the particular unease of being in an enclosed space with a man he did not know well. By now the fear often arrived before the trigger was fully clear, and the trigger seemed to be everywhere once the fear had started.

Kwame finally sought help after realizing how much his life had contracted in a job that required him to move through office suites, meet new clients, and tolerate unpredictable interruptions. He was exhausted by how often he startled, how quickly strangers felt dangerous, and how impossible it was becoming to separate the present from those sensory fragments of the assault. He is afraid that if he cannot get control of this, he will keep organizing his entire life around doors, voices, and the presence of men. What he hopes for, though he says it cautiously, is to be able to walk into a room, hear a door close, and remain in the room he is actually in.
